title: Psenicska v. Twentieth Century Fox Film Corp. — district court
lead: Participants in Borat say the filmmakers deceived them about the production and rushed them into signing. Three related suits turn on releases and specific disclaimers about the very film characteristics and identities allegedly misrepresented.

actors.name: Cindy Streit and her dinner guests
actors.role: Etiquette provider and participants in a filmed dinner.

actors.name: Todd Lewis Schulman and Sacha Baron Cohen
actors.role: Production contact and actor playing Borat.

actors.name: Twentieth Century Fox and other filmmaking defendants
actors.role: Parties seeking dismissal based on consent agreements.

proceedings: Psenicska, Streit and associated plaintiffs, and Martin filed separate actions; the Alabama Streit action was transferred to New York.
Judge Preska granted all three Rule 12(b)(6) dismissal motions, closed the actions, and denied pending motions as moot.
limits: This transforms the canonical district-court brief without a fresh audit or later-treatment certification. Deception and filming events remained allegations accepted at dismissal, not trial findings. The later appellate analysis is a separate decision and is not attributed here. Streit’s later release was additional background, not the common ground disposing of all cases.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Psenicska agrees to help with a supposed documentary
paragraphs: Michael Psenicska had run a driving school for thirty-two years when Todd Lewis Schulman contacted him in May 2005 about a documentary on foreigners’ integration into American life. Psenicska agreed to meet a crew in Washington, D.C., June 13, warning that he had to leave by 5 p.m. for a 6 p.m. class.

His complaint alleged that the crew arrived ninety minutes late with $500 and papers described as necessary for the documentary. Unexpectedly asked to sign, without his reading glasses and feeling rushed, he signed the Standard Consent Agreement unread in reliance on earlier conversations.

During filming, actor Sacha Baron Cohen as Borat allegedly drove erratically and made derogatory remarks. Psenicska accused apparent producers of setting him up and later unsuccessfully sought an explanation from Schulman. He sued December 3, 2007.

sections.title: A dinner arranged by Streit becomes another filmed encounter
paragraphs: Cindy Streit owned an etiquette-training business, identified as ETS. She alleged that Schulman requested training for a Belarus dignitary and a dinner for an educational documentary intended for Belarus television. Streit and Springland Films signed a services agreement October 24, 2005. Plans changed so Borat would skip training but attend dinner.

Guests included Sarah Moseley, Ben McKinnon, Michael Jared, and Lynn Jared. Plaintiffs alleged a late crew arrival and rushed presentation of consents immediately before Borat’s arrival; each signed. Borat allegedly made sexist comments and introduced a woman as a prostitute. The resulting film showed departures and insinuated racial intolerance.

After filming but before suit, Streit, ETS, and Springland signed another release: Streit received $4,450 for releasing claims of herself or ETS against Springland and related entities. The Streit plaintiffs later sued in Alabama; their case moved to the Southern District of New York in February 2008.

sections.title: Martin gives dining instruction under a similar alleged premise
sections.cue: How did she learn who had appeared?
paragraphs: Kathie Martin operated the Etiquette Training School of Birmingham. She alleged an agreement to instruct a foreign reporter being filmed for Belarus television. When Schulman learned that her husband knew another Cohen character from Da Ali G Show, he allegedly postponed filming to reduce recognition risk.

At the rescheduled session, Martin received $350 and signed what Schulman called a standard filming release. Cohen allegedly made sexist and anti-Semitic comments and displayed nude photographs of his supposed son. The director apologized for the photographs. Martin’s husband later identified Cohen, and her efforts to reach Schulman failed. She sued in February 2008.

sections.title: The defendants invoke materially identical written consents
sections.cue: What did the agreements actually cover?
paragraphs: The filmmaking defendants moved under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6). Judge Loretta Preska accepted material allegations and favorable reasonable inferences but could consider incorporated agreements known to plaintiffs and relied on in suit without converting dismissal into a trial.

Psenicska’s form named One America; the others named Springland. Each consented to a documentary-style motion picture for young adults using entertaining content and formats. Waivers identified publicity and likeness claims, intrusion, prima facie tort, and fraud involving deception or surprise about the film or agreement. Martin’s also specifically covered sexually oriented materials or activities.

Paragraph 5 specifically denied reliance on statements about the nature of the film and identities of participants or others involved. This was more targeted than a general merger provision excluding outside contractual terms.

sections.title: The film fits the unambiguous documentary-style description
sections.cue: Why did fictional comedy not defeat the releases?
paragraphs: Plaintiffs argued that documentary-style was ambiguous or excluded Borat. Under the undisputed New York choice-of-law clause, ambiguity was a legal threshold determined in contractual context and relevant usage. Disagreement or strained alternatives did not create it.

Psenicska supplied, and other parties accepted, a definition referring to characteristics of a film providing a factual record or report. The dispute concerned what fit the category, not competing reasonable definitions. “Style” mattered: a fictional character could interact with real interviewees and events in documentary form.

Borat used real people and events within its fictional protagonist’s journey; that contrast helped create its effect. Humor likewise did not remove documentary style, as examples of humorous documentaries illustrated. The consents therefore applied unambiguously and could be enforced on the pleadings.

sections.title: Specific nonreliance defeats the alleged fraudulent-inducement escape
sections.cue: Why did superior knowledge not save these pleadings?
paragraphs: Fraudulent inducement under the applied New York rule required knowing material misrepresentation or omission, intent, reasonable reliance, and resulting harm. Plaintiffs said false descriptions of production and personnel induced signatures and characterized the merger clause as general.

The court applied Danann, a precedent allowing sufficiently specific disclaimers to defeat reliance on the disclaimed subject. Here Paragraph 5 addressed exactly film nature and participant identities. Plaintiffs could not plead reasonable reliance on those subjects after expressly disclaiming it. The waiver released substantive claim categories; nonreliance defeated the attempted fraud-based escape. The reasoning did not say every signed release defeats every fraud claim.

Plaintiffs also invoked a disclosure duty and an exception for facts peculiarly within defendants’ knowledge. Recasting the same film and identity representations as omissions did not supply reliance negated by these terms. The court did not declare superior knowledge universally irrelevant and did not reach other defense arguments after resolving these grounds.

sections.title: All three actions are dismissed
sections.cue: What did the order decide about the alleged deception?
paragraphs: On September 3, 2008, Preska granted dismissal in Psenicska, Streit, and Martin, directed closure of each action, and denied all pending motions as moot. Defendants received no damages award.

The judgment enforced these agreements against these pleaded claims. It did not find after trial that the plaintiffs’ descriptions were false or announce unrestricted permission for filmmakers to deceive participants.
